results.title: Japan Caught Between China, Russia and Trump's Changing World Order
results.description: Japan faces one of its most difficult diplomatic challenges in decades as US President Donald Trump pursues closer engagement with China and Russia, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi struggles to repair relations with Beijing, and a changing international order raises questions about Tokyo's ability to protect its security and economic interests without being excluded from decisions made by the world's largest powers. The challenge became particularly visible at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, where Trump held talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin while Takaichi failed to secure a formal bilateral meeting with Xi, despite traveling to China for the first time since a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan severely damaged relations between Tokyo and Beijing. The three-way meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin attracted international attention not only because of the issues discussed but also because of its implications for countries that depend on the United States for security while maintaining complicated economic and political relationships with China. Trump described the gathering as bigger than the historic Yalta Conference of 1945, invoking the wartime meeting that helped shape the postwar international order. For Japan, the comparison carries particular significance. Tokyo has spent decades building its foreign policy around the US-Japan security alliance, a rules-based international system and the assumption that Washington would consult closely with its Asian allies when addressing major regional security questions. The prospect of Washington reaching understandings with Beijing and Moscow without Japanese participation has therefore become a growing concern among policymakers. Japan's immediate diplomatic problem remains its deteriorating relationship with China, which has continued for more than a year following remarks by Takaichi in November 2025 suggesting that a Chinese military blockade of Taiwan could constitute a situation threatening Japan's survival and potentially justify the exercise of collective self-defense. The comments represented a more explicit description of Japan's possible response to a Taiwan conflict than previous governments had generally been willing to provide. Beijing reacted strongly, demanding that Takaichi withdraw her remarks and subsequently increasing diplomatic and economic pressure on Japan. Chinese measures have included restrictions affecting exports of strategically important materials, warnings discouraging travel to Japan and tighter controls on critical minerals used in automobiles, electronics, semiconductor manufacturing and defense equipment. These developments have exposed Japan's vulnerability to economic coercion at a time when its manufacturers are already struggling with rising costs and uncertainty in international trade. Although Japan and China remain deeply connected through trade and investment, the political relationship has become increasingly difficult to manage. China is one of Japan's largest trading partners, and Japanese companies have extensive manufacturing operations and commercial interests in the Chinese market. At the Shenzhen summit, Takaichi attempted to reduce tensions by reaffirming that Japan's position on Taiwan remained consistent with the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communique, which established the framework for the normalization of diplomatic relations between the two countries. She emphasized that Tokyo's fundamental position had not changed and declined to explain how Japan might respond to a hypothetical military conflict involving Taiwan. The statements suggested an effort to return to a more cautious diplomatic approach while avoiding any formal retreat from her previous security assessments. However, the gesture did not produce the high-level engagement Tokyo had hoped for. Although Takaichi and Xi exchanged greetings and shook hands during summit events, the Chinese leader did not hold a formal meeting with her. The contrast with China's reception of other major leaders was striking. Beijing gave Trump and Putin prominent attention, while Takaichi received a comparatively restrained welcome, reinforcing concerns that China was deliberately demonstrating Japan's reduced diplomatic influence. Nevertheless, Takaichi maintained that communication with Beijing remained important and that Japan would continue seeking opportunities to stabilize bilateral relations. The dispute over Taiwan extends beyond diplomatic protocol. Japan's southwestern islands lie close to Taiwan, with Yonaguni Island located approximately 110 kilometers from the Taiwanese coast. Any military conflict in the Taiwan Strait could directly affect Japanese territory, commercial shipping routes, US military facilities in Japan and the movement of energy supplies through the region. China regards Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to achieve unification. Japan, while maintaining diplomatic relations with Beijing rather than Taipei, has repeatedly emphasized the importance of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. The United States remains central to Japan's security calculations, but Trump's approach to international relations has introduced uncertainty into an alliance that has traditionally provided the foundation for Tokyo's defense policy. Trump has increasingly emphasized direct negotiations between major powers, often prioritizing trade agreements, strategic bargaining and immediate national interests over the established practices of multilateral diplomacy. His engagement with Xi and Putin has raised questions about whether Washington could pursue arrangements on security, trade or regional influence that might not fully reflect Japanese interests. Following the Shenzhen summit, Takaichi held a telephone conversation with Trump on November 19 lasting approximately 20 minutes. The leaders discussed developments in the Indo-Pacific, the war in Ukraine and international affairs following Trump's meetings with the Chinese and Russian presidents. Takaichi reiterated her intention to strengthen the US-Japan alliance and maintain close coordination with Washington. However, the fact that Japan was receiving explanations of discussions among the three major powers rather than participating directly highlighted the diplomatic limitations facing Tokyo. Differences between Washington and Tokyo were also evident over international institutions. Takaichi reaffirmed Japan's support for the International Criminal Court after the United States, China and Russia criticized the institution in a joint declaration issued in Shenzhen. The disagreement illustrated a broader tension between Japan's traditional commitment to international rules and institutions and an emerging approach to global politics in which the largest military and economic powers seek to negotiate directly with one another. At the same time, Japan faces renewed financial pressure from Washington over the cost of maintaining American military forces on Japanese territory. The Trump administration has reportedly demanded that Tokyo increase its host-nation support for US forces to approximately 3 trillion yen over five years beginning in fiscal 2027, roughly three times the current arrangement. Under the existing five-year agreement ending in March 2027, Japan's contribution totals approximately 1.06 trillion yen, or about 210 billion yen annually. The request comes as Japan is already undertaking a major expansion of its own defense capabilities, placing additional pressure on public finances and raising questions about how much Tokyo should spend maintaining the American military presence. Japan has accelerated its efforts to strengthen defense capabilities, including acquiring longer-range weapons, expanding missile defense systems and improving its ability to respond to threats around its southwestern islands. The Takaichi government has also moved forward with a review of Japan's three principal security documents, including the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program, with revisions expected before the end of 2026. The review has generated debate over issues that were once considered politically difficult, including restrictions on the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japanese territory and the possible acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines. Japan's longstanding Three Non-Nuclear Principles prohibit possessing, producing or permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons. Any significant revision to those principles would represent a major change in the country's postwar security policy and would likely provoke domestic controversy and international scrutiny. The government must therefore balance demands for stronger deterrence against constitutional, political and historical constraints that continue to shape Japanese attitudes toward military power. Relations with Russia present another challenge, although the Shenzhen summit produced an unexpected diplomatic opening. Takaichi held talks with Putin on November 18 for approximately 30 minutes, marking the first meeting between Japanese and Russian leaders in seven years and the first since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The discussions focused partly on the detention of a Japanese national in Russia and the treatment of Japanese companies operating in the country. The meeting did not represent a broader normalization of relations, but it suggested that Tokyo was willing to maintain limited direct communication with Moscow despite continuing disagreements over Ukraine and territorial issues. Japan has joined Western countries in imposing sanctions on Russia over the invasion of Ukraine and has provided substantial financial and humanitarian assistance to Kyiv. Tokyo's position reflects concerns that allowing territorial changes through military force in Europe could weaken international opposition to similar actions in East Asia. The longstanding territorial dispute over four Russian-controlled islands north of Hokkaido, which Japan refers to as the Northern Territories, remains unresolved. The disagreement has prevented the two countries from concluding a formal peace treaty ending World War II. Tensions intensified following Putin's visit to one of the disputed islands in August 2026, while Russia's increasing military cooperation with China and North Korea has added further complications. Japan lodged a protest in November after two suspected Russian military aircraft violated Japanese airspace near the country's southwestern region. Russian military activity around Japan and Taiwan has become a growing concern for defense officials, particularly as Moscow expands its strategic coordination with Beijing. North Korea's nuclear and missile programs represent another persistent threat. Pyongyang's development of increasingly sophisticated weapons, combined with its strengthening military relationship with Russia, has reinforced Tokyo's determination to improve deterrence and regional security cooperation. The issue of Japanese nationals abducted by North Korean agents decades ago also remains a significant political priority. Takaichi has indicated that she is prepared to pursue diplomatic avenues, including the possibility of a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, to secure progress on the unresolved cases. Against this increasingly complicated international backdrop, Japan has sought to strengthen relations with South Korea, a country that shares many of its security concerns but has historically experienced tensions with Tokyo over wartime history and territorial disputes. Takaichi met South Korean President Lee Jae Myung in Manila on November 17, marking their fourth bilateral summit since she took office in October 2025. The two leaders welcomed improvements in bilateral relations and agreed to strengthen cooperation on supply chains, energy security and regional stability. Lee said public sentiment between the two countries had improved significantly, while Takaichi emphasized the growing importance of their relationship as international security conditions become more challenging. South Korea and Japan remain important partners in the American alliance network in Northeast Asia, particularly in monitoring North Korean missile launches and coordinating responses to regional security threats. However, both governments also face pressure to maintain workable relations with China, making diplomatic flexibility essential. The leaders agreed to continue their regular summit exchanges, with Lee expected to visit Japan in January 2027. Japan has also intensified its engagement with Southeast Asia, where governments are increasingly concerned about becoming dependent on either Washington or Beijing. At the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Takaichi promoted stronger economic resilience, supply-chain diversification and energy security, arguing that regional countries should have greater freedom to make decisions without external coercion. Japan's approach reflects a recognition that its influence in Asia cannot depend exclusively on military cooperation with the United States. Through infrastructure investment, development assistance, technology partnerships and financial support, Tokyo has sought to establish itself as a reliable economic partner for Southeast Asian countries. The Philippines has emerged as an especially important security partner because of its location near Taiwan and its disputes with China over maritime territory in the South China Sea. During talks with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on November 16, Takaichi welcomed an agreement to provide defense equipment through Japan's Official Security Assistance program. The two governments also discussed maritime security, North Korea, regional energy cooperation and efforts to strengthen economic links through the Luzon Economic Corridor. Japan's expanding cooperation with Manila forms part of a broader strategy to support maritime security and protect shipping routes connecting the Pacific and Indian oceans. The importance of these routes extends far beyond military considerations. Japan imports most of its oil and natural gas, making uninterrupted access to international shipping essential for its economic stability. Disruption in the Middle East has increased the urgency of energy security cooperation, particularly as tensions around Iran and regional shipping routes affect global supply conditions. At the Asia Zero Emission Community leaders' meeting on November 17, Takaichi proposed a new regional oil security initiative designed to coordinate energy reserves and strengthen responses to supply disruptions. The initiative would work alongside a Philippine-led oil stockpiling arrangement and could provide Asian economies with a mechanism comparable in some respects to the International Energy Agency. Japan's engagement with Southeast Asia is also closely connected to its efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese suppliers of strategically important materials. Rare earth elements and other critical minerals are essential for electric vehicles, industrial machinery, renewable energy systems and advanced military technology. Chinese export restrictions have demonstrated how economic dependence can become a source of political vulnerability, prompting Tokyo to accelerate cooperation with Australia, Canada, European countries and Southeast Asian partners. During the November 17 Quad summit in Manila, Takaichi joined Trump, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in reaffirming their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific. The four leaders expressed opposition to unilateral attempts to change the regional status quo through force or coercion and emphasized the importance of securing critical supply chains. They also agreed to expand cooperation in maritime surveillance, technology, energy security and humanitarian assistance. Under the partnership's maritime surveillance initiatives, patrol aircraft from the four countries are expected to conduct a joint maritime exercise in 2027, marking another step toward more practical security cooperation. Although the Quad is not a formal military alliance, it has become an important framework for countries seeking to maintain regional stability without relying exclusively on bilateral security arrangements. Japan is simultaneously strengthening its security relationships with European partners. A major example is its joint development of a next-generation fighter aircraft with Britain and Italy, a project intended to improve military technology, share development costs and strengthen defense-industrial cooperation among the three countries. The initiative represents a significant expansion of Japan's international defense partnerships and reflects a gradual shift away from restrictions that historically limited its participation in overseas military equipment programs. Closer relations with European countries also serve Japan's economic security interests, particularly in developing alternative sources of critical minerals and advanced technologies. However, the increasingly complex network of partnerships does not eliminate Japan's dependence on the United States for extended nuclear deterrence and major military capabilities. Nor does it resolve the economic reality that China remains an indispensable market and manufacturing center for many Japanese companies. This creates a difficult strategic balance. Tokyo must strengthen its defenses against potential military threats while avoiding economic confrontation severe enough to damage Japanese industry, employment and growth. The challenge is particularly acute in the semiconductor, automotive and electronics sectors, where supply chains cross national borders and depend on materials and components produced in several countries. The possibility of a prolonged confrontation between Japan and China could accelerate investment outside China, but shifting production networks requires substantial capital and time. Japanese manufacturers also face uncertainty over American trade policy, including tariffs and other restrictions introduced under Trump. As Washington and Beijing negotiate directly, Tokyo must consider the possibility that commercial arrangements between the two countries could alter competitive conditions for Japanese companies without addressing Japan's concerns over economic security. The result is a foreign-policy environment in which traditional distinctions between diplomacy, national defense and economic management are becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. For Takaichi, the central challenge is to preserve Japan's influence without being drawn into an escalating confrontation between the major powers. Her government's stronger national security posture has attracted support from those who argue that Japan must respond more decisively to China's military expansion and North Korea's weapons development. Others have warned that excessively confrontational diplomacy could weaken Japan's economic position and reduce the opportunities available for negotiation, particularly when Washington is pursuing its own relationship with Beijing. The events in Shenzhen demonstrated the risks associated with both approaches. Japan's refusal to retreat from its security concerns has contributed to a prolonged diplomatic confrontation with China, yet Washington's willingness to negotiate directly with Beijing and Moscow has shown that alignment with the United States does not guarantee participation in every major international decision. At the same time, Takaichi's meetings with Putin, Lee and Southeast Asian leaders demonstrated that Tokyo retains considerable diplomatic options beyond its immediate relationship with China. Japan's economic size, technological capabilities, development financing and extensive international partnerships continue to give it influence across the Indo-Pacific and beyond. The question is whether those advantages can be translated into a coherent strategy capable of protecting Japanese interests as the international order becomes more fragmented. The coming months will be particularly important as Tokyo finalizes its revised security strategy, negotiates the future cost of hosting American forces and seeks to restore communication with Beijing ahead of the 55th anniversary of the normalization of Japan-China diplomatic relations in 2027. For Japan, the greatest danger may not be an immediate breakdown of any single alliance or diplomatic relationship, but the gradual emergence of an international system in which major powers make decisions over regional security and economic arrangements while smaller and middle-sized countries struggle to influence the outcome. Avoiding that prospect will require Tokyo to maintain its American alliance, stabilize relations with China, strengthen cooperation with neighboring countries and expand its network of economic and security partnerships. The Shenzhen summit has underscored how difficult that task has become, leaving Japan to confront an increasingly important question: whether it can remain a significant architect of regional stability or must adapt to an international order increasingly shaped by decisions made in Washington, Beijing and Moscow. (News On Japan)
